author: D

components.title: Compute committee count
components.what: Count committees with exactly 3, 4, or 5 women: C(5,3)C(9,2) + C(5,4)C(9,1) + C(5,5)C(9,0). Show this working briefly and evaluate the sum.

components.title: Format final response
components.what: End with exactly one line of the form FINAL: <answer>, using digits only for the numerical answer and no commas, units, or extra text on that final line.

log.author: A
log.draft:
Working: Break into cases by number of women (3, 4, or 5), since the committee has 5 seats total.

- 3 women, 2 men: C(5,3)·C(9,2) = 10·36 = 360
- 4 women, 1 man: C(5,4)·C(9,1) = 5·9 = 45
- 5 women, 0 men: C(5,5)·C(9,0) = 1·1 = 1

Sum: 360 + 45 + 1 = 406

Check via complement: total committees C(14,5) = 2002. Complement (0, 1, or 2 women) = C(5,0)C(9,5) + C(5,1)C(9,4) + C(5,2)C(9,3) = 126 + 630 + 840 = 1596. Then 2002 − 1596 = 406, matching the direct sum.

FINAL: 406

challenges.problem: There is no substantive mathematical error under the standard interpretation that a committee is an unordered selection. The only implicit assumption is that member order or assigned roles do not matter.

asked: The record notes the only implicit assumption is that committee selections are unordered with no assigned roles; what in the problem statement supports that reading, and would the intended answer change under any plausible alternative reading?

Both the direct case sum and the complement check rely on C(14,5)=2002 and the individual binomial values; can you state the source or explicit computation for C(9,5)=126, C(9,4)=126 vs 630 (i.e., C(5,1)C(9,4)), and C(5,2)C(9,3)=840, so each complement term is independently verifiable?
Edge case: does 'at least 3 women' unambiguously exclude any committee with 2 or fewer women, and is the 5-women case (only 1 way, leaving 0 men) legitimately a valid 5-member committee here?
replies: The problem statement says 'choose a committee of 5 members'; a committee is normally a set of members, with no roles, offices, or ordering mentioned, so the unordered combination reading is supported. Under a plausible alternative reading in which the 5 selected members are assigned distinct roles or are ordered, each unordered committee could be arranged in 5! ways, changing the answer to 406 × 120 = 48720.

Using C(n,k) = n!/(k!(n-k)!): C(9,5) = 9!/(5!4!) = 126. C(9,4) = 9!/(4!5!) = 126, so the complement term for 1 woman and 4 men is C(5,1)C(9,4) = 5 × 126 = 630, not C(9,4) alone. C(5,2) = 10 and C(9,3) = 9!/(3!6!) = (9×8×7)/(3×2×1) = 84, so C(5,2)C(9,3) = 10 × 84 = 840. No external source; these are direct binomial-coefficient computations.

Yes, 'at least 3 women' means the number of women is ≥ 3, so committees with 0, 1, or 2 women are unambiguously excluded. The 5-women case is valid: there are exactly 5 women available, so choosing all 5 women and 0 men is a legitimate 5-member committee, with C(5,5) = 1 and C(9,0) = 1.
open: The complement terms C(9,5)=126, C(5,1)C(9,4)=630 and C(5,2)C(9,3)=840 are now shown by explicit factorial computation, but the total C(14,5)=2002 used in the complement check, and the direct-case factors C(5,3)=10, C(9,2)=36, C(5,4)=5, C(9,1)=9, are still asserted without shown computation, so the arithmetic identity 2002-1596=406 is not yet independently verifiable end to end.

asked: Please show the explicit computation of C(14,5) and of the direct-case factors C(5,3), C(9,2), C(5,4), C(9,1), and confirm that 126+630+840=1596 and 2002-1596=406 arithmetically.
